Lumio — Data Analytics Capstone Project¶

See what your systems are hiding: detecting silent payment failures with statistics, regression, time series, machine learning and Monte Carlo simulation¶
Project type End-to-end data analytics project (CRISP-DM)
Domain Digital payments operations (banking / fintech)
Data 31 days of payment telemetry: 3-week training history (17 Jan – 6 Feb 2025) + 10-day live period (7 – 16 Feb 2025), 48 segments, 5-minute grain, ~430,000 rows. Rhythm and three real anomalies from the Numenta Anomaly Benchmark (NAB)
Tools Python · pandas · SQL (SQLite) · SciPy · statsmodels · scikit-learn · matplotlib / seaborn
Companion app The Lumio live demo (../run_local.py), which uses the same dataset and runs these methods in real time

How to run: pip install -r requirements.txt, then open this notebook in Jupyter or VS Code and choose Run All (about 2–3 minutes). Every number in the text below is computed by the code; nothing is typed in by hand.

0. Project framing (CRISP-DM)¶

This project follows CRISP-DM (Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining), the most widely used framework for analytics projects:

CRISP-DM phase Where it happens in this project
1. Business understanding Section 0: problem, stakeholders, questions, success criteria
2. Data understanding Sections 1, 3: sources, dictionary, EDA
3. Data preparation Section 2: quality checks, cleaning, aggregation, feature engineering
4. Modelling Sections 5–11: statistics, regression, time series, classification, ML, clustering, simulation
5. Evaluation Sections 6.4, 7.5, 8, 9, 11: accuracy, precision/recall, cross-validation, business value
6. Deployment The Lumio live app: the same models running on streaming data, with alerts e-mailed to teams

0.1 Business problem¶

Banks lose money and customers to "silent" payment failures: problems that never trip a technical alarm because every server is "up", yet payments slow down, fail, or quietly vanish for one slice of customers (one bank, one app version, one region). Fixed-threshold monitoring either misses them or floods teams with false alarms, especially when normal demand swings by 10× between 4 am and 6 pm, on weekends, on payday, or during a storm.

0.2 Stakeholders¶

Stakeholder What they need
Operations / SRE Fewer, more accurate alerts, with a probable cause
Product & Release teams To know quickly when a new app version hurts payments
Fraud & Risk Early sign of attacks (e.g. card-testing bots)
Business Operations To tell demand changes (storm, payday) apart from faults
Leadership Money at risk and the return on investment (ROI) of the tool

0.3 Analytical questions → hypotheses¶

# Question Hypothesis tested Section
Q1 What does "normal" look like? Volume and payment time follow daily and weekly seasonality 3, 7
Q2 Do payment channels, platforms and banks behave differently? H₀: mean payment time is equal across groups 5
Q3 What drives payment time? Payment time depends on channel, bank, hour, load and upstream services 6, 9
Q4 Can we forecast demand? A seasonal model beats a naive forecast 7
Q5 Can we detect real incidents without flooding teams? A model on expected vs actual beats a fixed threshold on precision and recall 8
Q6 Are there natural groups of segments? Segments cluster by behaviour 10
Q7 Is it worth it? Faster detection reduces annual losses by more than the tool costs 11

0.4 Success criteria (set before modelling)¶

  • Statistical: regression R² on unseen data ≥ 0.5; forecast MAPE ≤ 10 % on normal days.
  • Detection: catch every planted incident in the test period with fewer false alarms than a fixed-threshold rule.
  • Business: positive expected net benefit in the Monte Carlo simulation, with a stated probability.

0.5 Scope & assumptions¶

  • The unit of analysis is a segment × 5-minute bucket (aggregated telemetry, no customer-level or personal data).
  • The answer key (planted events) is used only for evaluation, never for training the detection rules, just as in the live app.
  • Monetary assumptions in Section 11 are clearly labelled and tested with sensitivity analysis.

1. Data understanding¶

1.1 Sources¶

File Rows What it is
payments_history_3weeks.csv.gz ~290 k Training history: 17 Jan – 6 Feb 2025, normal operations
payments_demo_10days.csv.gz ~139 k Live period: 7 – 16 Feb 2025 (6 business days + 2 weekends), contains the anomalies
services_*.csv.gz ~60 k Upstream services (UPI switch, card network, fraud check, 4 core-banking systems)
answer_key.csv 19 The planted events: used only to evaluate
feeds.csv 6 Deploy feed and change calendar (context a real analyst would also have)

Provenance. Volume follows the real NYC-taxi demand trace from the Numenta Anomaly Benchmark (MIT licence), including the real January 2015 blizzard. Two services follow real NAB server traces (an EC2 system failure and an RDS CPU level shift). The payments themselves are simulated on top of these real rhythms, so the ground truth is known exactly. This is what makes rigorous evaluation possible.

segment text Bank · Channel · Platform · Region Bank X · UPI · Android · North

Why p95 and not the average? Payment times are right-skewed: a few very slow payments ruin the customer experience but barely move the mean. The 95th percentile is the industry-standard service-level indicator (SLI).

2. Data quality & preparation¶

Good analysis starts with trustworthy data. We check completeness, uniqueness, validity and consistency, the standard data-quality dimensions.

In [3]:
def dq_profile(df, name):
    k = ["ts"] + SEG + ["app_version"]
    seg_per_ts = df.drop_duplicates(["ts"] + SEG).groupby("ts").size()
    return pd.Series({
        "rows": len(df),
        "missing values (nulls)": int(df.isna().sum().sum()),
        "duplicate records": int(df.duplicated(k).sum()),
        "timestamps": df.ts.nunique(),
        "timestamps with < 48 segments reporting": int((seg_per_ts < 48).sum()),
        "invalid: success > volume": int((df.success_count > df.volume).sum()),
        "invalid: volume ≤ 0": int((df.volume <= 0).sum()),
        "invalid: p95 ≤ 0": int((df.p95_ms <= 0).sum()),
    }, name=name)

# Outliers (IQR rule) in normal history: are they errors or real behaviour?
def iqr_outliers(s):
    q1, q3 = s.quantile([.25, .75]); iqr = q3 - q1
    return (s < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (s > q3 + 1.5 * iqr)
out = hist_raw.groupby("channel")["p95_ms"].transform(iqr_outliers)
print(f"IQR outliers in p95 (history): {out.mean():.2%} of rows")
print(hist_raw[out].groupby("hour" if "hour" in hist_raw else hist_raw.ts.dt.hour).size().sort_values(ascending=False).head(5).rename("outlier rows by hour"))

IQR outliers in p95 (history): 1.54% of rows

Name: outlier rows by hour, dtype: int64

Decisions (documented, as in a real project):

  1. Duplicates → removed. Counting the same payments twice would inflate volume and could invent an anomaly.
  2. Missing windows → not filled with zeros. A zero would look like "all payments vanished", a false alarm. They are left missing and reported to the data team. (The live app does exactly this: it holds the data and raises a data ticket, not a page.)
  3. IQR outliers → kept. They cluster at the busy hours: they are real peak-time behaviour, not errors. Deleting them would teach the model that peaks don't exist.
  4. App-version rows → during a rollout one segment reports two versions. For segment-level analysis we combine them with volume-weighted averages; for the root-cause test (5.4) we keep them separate.
In [6]:
def prepare(df, period):
    df = df.drop_duplicates(["ts"] + SEG + ["app_version"]).copy()
    df["w_p95"], df["w_amt"] = df.p95_ms * df.volume, df.avg_amount * df.volume
    g = df.groupby(["ts"] + SEG, as_index=False).agg(volume=("volume", "sum"), success_count=("success_count", "sum"),
                                                     w_p95=("w_p95", "sum"), w_amt=("w_amt", "sum"))
    g["p95_ms"], g["avg_amount"] = g.w_p95 / g.volume, g.w_amt / g.volume
    g = g.drop(columns=["w_p95", "w_amt"])
    g["failed"] = g.volume - g.success_count
    g["success_rate"] = g.success_count / g.volume
    g["hour"], g["dow"] = g.ts.dt.hour, g.ts.dt.dayofweek
    g["weekday"] = g.ts.dt.day_name().str[:3]
    g["is_weekend"] = (g.dow >= 5).astype(int)
    g["date"] = g.ts.dt.normalize()
    is_payday = g.date.isin(pd.to_datetime(["2025-01-31", "2025-02-14"]))   # 15th / month-end, moved to Friday
    g["payday_evening"] = (is_payday & g.hour.between(16, 22)).astype(int)
    g["log_p95"], g["log_volume"] = np.log(g.p95_ms), np.log(g.volume)
    g["segment"] = g.bank + " · " + g.channel + " · " + g.platform + " · " + g.region
    g["period"] = period
    return g

hist, live = prepare(hist_raw, "history"), prepare(demo_raw, "live")
pay = pd.concat([hist, live], ignore_index=True)
for c in SEG + ["segment"]: pay[c] = pay[c].astype("category")
hist, live = pay[pay.period == "history"].copy(), pay[pay.period == "live"].copy()

# Mask of rows touched by any planted event (used ONLY for evaluation / "normal-only" test sets)
def in_scope(df, scope):
    m = np.ones(len(df), bool)
    for k, v in scope.items(): m &= (df[k] == v).values
    return m
def event_mask(df, kinds=None, pad="0min"):
    m = np.zeros(len(df), bool)
    for _, e in key.iterrows():
        if kinds and e.kind not in kinds: continue
        m |= in_scope(df, e.scope) & ((df.ts >= e.start - pd.Timedelta(pad)) & (df.ts < e.end + pd.Timedelta(pad))).values
    return m
live["any_event"] = event_mask(live, pad="30min")
print(f"Clean segment-level table: {len(pay):,} rows | live rows touched by a planted event: {live.any_event.mean():.1%}")

Clean segment-level table: 428,408 rows | live rows touched by a planted event: 21.2%

EDA findings

  • Strong daily and weekly seasonality in volume (the peak-to-trough ratio above), so "normal" must be time-aware.
  • Card is slower than UPI and carries higher payment values. Android is slightly slower than iOS. Bank W is the slowest bank.
  • p95 is right-skewed (skew > 0), so we model log(p95) in regression.
  • Success rate is very stable (~98 %), so small drops matter and need statistical rather than eyeball thresholds.
  • avg_amount correlates with p95 overall (≈ 0.56), but is this causal? Section 6.1 shows it is confounding by channel.

4. SQL analysis¶

The cleaned data is loaded into a SQLite database (the live app uses SQLite or PostgreSQL). These queries are the kind an analyst writes daily.

In [13]:
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
cols = ["ts", "bank", "channel", "platform", "region", "volume", "success_count", "failed", "p95_ms", "avg_amount", "period"]
t = pay[cols].copy(); t["ts"] = t.ts.dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
for c in SEG: t[c] = t[c].astype(str)
t.to_sql("payments", con, index=False)

con.execute("CREATE INDEX ix_p ON payments(ts, bank, channel)"); con.execute("CREATE INDEX ix_s ON services(ts, service)")
def q(sql): return pd.read_sql_query(sql, con)

FROM payments
WHERE period = 'history'

5. Hypothesis testing¶

Each test states H₀ / H₁, checks assumptions, reports the p-value and an effect size. With hundreds of thousands of rows almost any difference is "statistically significant", so the effect size tells us whether it matters.

To reduce dependence between consecutive 5-minute rows, tests 5.1–5.3 use segment × hour averages (independent-enough units, n ≈ 24 k).

In [20]:
hh = (hist.assign(hr=hist.ts.dt.floor("h"))
          .groupby(["hr"] + SEG, observed=True)
          .agg(p95_ms=("p95_ms", "mean"), volume=("volume", "sum"), success_count=("success_count", "sum"), failed=("failed", "sum"))
          .reset_index())
def cohens_d(a, b): return (a.mean() - b.mean()) / np.sqrt((a.var(ddof=1) + b.var(ddof=1)) / 2)
def verdict(p, alpha=.05): return "**reject H₀**" if p < alpha else "**fail to reject H₀**"
print(f"Hourly units: {len(hh):,}")

Hourly units: 24,192

5.1 Two-sample t-test (Welch) — Android vs iOS payment time¶

H₀: μ_Android = μ_iOS · H₁: μ_Android ≠ μ_iOS · α = 0.05

In [21]:
a, b = hh[hh.platform == "Android"].p95_ms, hh[hh.platform == "iOS"].p95_ms
t, p = stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)
lev = stats.levene(a, b)
d = cohens_d(a, b)
RESULTS["t_android_ios"] = (a.mean() - b.mean(), p, d)
say(f"Android mean **{a.mean():.0f} ms**, iOS **{b.mean():.0f} ms** (difference {a.mean()-b.mean():+.0f} ms). "
    f"Levene test for equal variances p = {lev.pvalue:.3g} → Welch's t-test (does not assume equal variances).  \n"
    f"t = {t:.2f}, p = {p:.3g} → {verdict(p)}. Cohen's d = **{d:.2f}** "
    f"({'small' if abs(d) < .5 else 'medium' if abs(d) < .8 else 'large'} effect).")

Android mean 2413 ms, iOS 2295 ms (difference +118 ms). Levene test for equal variances p = 6.42e-07 → Welch's t-test (does not assume equal variances).
t = 26.28, p = 4.05e-150 → reject H₀. Cohen's d = 0.34 (small effect).

5.2 Chi-square test of independence — does payment outcome depend on channel?¶

H₀: success/failure is independent of channel.

In [22]:
ct = hist.groupby("channel", observed=True)[["success_count", "failed"]].sum()
chi2, p, dof, exp = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)
n = ct.values.sum(); v = np.sqrt(chi2 / (n * (min(ct.shape) - 1)))
display(ct.assign(fail_pct=lambda d: 100 * d.failed / (d.failed + d.success_count)).round(3))
RESULTS["chi_channel"] = (p, v)
say(f"χ² = {chi2:,.1f}, dof = {dof}, p = {p:.3g} → {verdict(p)}. **Cramér's V = {v:.4f}** (negligible).  \n"
    "**Lesson: statistically significant ≠ practically significant.** With ~40 million payments even a tiny difference is 'significant'. "
    "The effect size shows it is too small to matter for operations.")
success_count failed fail_pct
channel
Card 14377033 280924 1.917
UPI 26188004 457463 1.717

χ² = 2,147.3, dof = 1, p = 0 → reject H₀. Cramér's V = 0.0072 (negligible).
Lesson: statistically significant ≠ practically significant. With ~40 million payments even a tiny difference is 'significant'. The effect size shows it is too small to matter for operations.

5.3 One-way ANOVA + Tukey HSD + Kruskal-Wallis — payment time across the four banks¶

H₀: μ_W = μ_X = μ_Y = μ_Z. ANOVA says whether some mean differs; Tukey HSD says which pairs; Kruskal-Wallis is the non-parametric check (no normality assumption).

In [23]:
groups = [g.p95_ms.values for _, g in hh.groupby("bank", observed=True)]
F, p = stats.f_oneway(*groups)
H, p_kw = stats.kruskal(*groups)
ss_between = sum(len(g) * (g.mean() - hh.p95_ms.mean())**2 for g in groups); ss_total = ((hh.p95_ms - hh.p95_ms.mean())**2).sum()
eta2 = ss_between / ss_total
RESULTS["anova_bank"] = (p, eta2)
eta_lbl = "large" if eta2 >= .14 else "medium" if eta2 >= .06 else "small" if eta2 >= .01 else "negligible"
say(f"ANOVA F = {F:,.1f}, p = {p:.3g} → {verdict(p)}; **η² = {eta2:.3f}**, a **{eta_lbl}** effect (bank explains {eta2:.1%} of the variation in hourly p95; Cohen's guide: 0.01 small, 0.06 medium, 0.14 large).  \n"
    f"Kruskal-Wallis H = {H:,.1f}, p = {p_kw:.3g}: same conclusion without assuming normality.")
tk = pairwise_tukeyhsd(hh.p95_ms, hh.bank.astype(str))
display(pd.DataFrame(tk.summary().data[1:], columns=tk.summary().data[0]))

ANOVA F = 1,694.1, p = 0 → reject H₀; η² = 0.174, a large effect (bank explains 17.4% of the variation in hourly p95; Cohen's guide: 0.01 small, 0.06 medium, 0.14 large).
Kruskal-Wallis H = 4,034.1, p = 0: same conclusion without assuming normality.

5.4 Root-cause test, as Lumio does it: is app v5.2 really slower than v5.1?¶

Live period, Bank X · UPI · Android, Friday 19:00–23:15, both versions running side by side (a natural A/B test).

  • Mann-Whitney U on payment time (non-parametric: p95 values are skewed)
  • Fisher's exact test on failures (2×2 table)
In [24]:
w = demo_raw[(demo_raw.bank == "Bank X") & (demo_raw.channel == "UPI") & (demo_raw.platform == "Android")
             & (demo_raw.ts >= "2025-02-07 19:00") & (demo_raw.ts < "2025-02-07 23:15")]
v51, v52 = w[w.app_version == 5.1].p95_ms, w[w.app_version == 5.2].p95_ms
U, p_mw = stats.mannwhitneyu(v52, v51, alternative="greater")
tab = w.assign(failed=w.volume - w.success_count).groupby("app_version")[["failed", "success_count"]].sum().loc[[5.2, 5.1]]
tab["fail %"] = (100 * tab.failed / (tab.failed + tab.success_count)).round(2)
odds, p_f = stats.fisher_exact(tab[["failed", "success_count"]].values)
RESULTS["release_ratio"] = v52.median() / v51.median()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
sns.boxplot(x=w.app_version.astype(str), y=w.p95_ms, palette=[TEAL, AMBER], ax=ax); ax.set(title="Bank X UPI Android, Fri 19:00–23:15", xlabel="app version", ylabel="p95 ms"); plt.show()
display(tab)
say(f"Median p95: v5.1 **{v51.median():.0f} ms** vs v5.2 **{v52.median():.0f} ms** → **{RESULTS['release_ratio']:.1f}× slower**.  \n"
    f"Mann-Whitney U = {U:,.0f}, one-sided p = {p_mw:.3g} → {verdict(p_mw)}.  \n"
    f"Fisher exact on failures: v5.2 failure rate {tab['fail %'].iloc[0]:.1f} % vs {tab['fail %'].iloc[1]:.1f} %, odds ratio = **{odds:.1f}**, p = {p_f:.3g} → {verdict(p_f)}.  \n"
    "This is exactly the check Lumio runs before it tells Release Management *'v5.2 is the cause'*. The claim is only made if the test passes.")
failed success_count fail %
app_version
5.2 2161 27248 7.35
5.1 918 50406 1.79

Median p95: v5.1 2124 ms vs v5.2 6878 ms → 3.2× slower.
Mann-Whitney U = 22,950, one-sided p = 1.76e-51 → reject H₀.
Fisher exact on failures: v5.2 failure rate 7.3 % vs 1.8 %, odds ratio = 4.4, p = 0 → reject H₀.
This is exactly the check Lumio runs before it tells Release Management 'v5.2 is the cause'. The claim is only made if the test passes.

5.5 Confidence intervals — why a quiet segment needs more evidence¶

Same success rate, very different certainty. Wilson 95 % intervals for one segment at 4 am vs 6 pm.

In [25]:
seg = hist[(hist.segment == "Bank Y · UPI · iOS · South")]
rows = []
for label, hr in [("04:00 (quiet)", 4), ("18:00 (busy)", 18)]:
    r = seg[seg.hour == hr].iloc[0]
    lo, hi = proportion_confint(r.success_count, r.volume, method="wilson")
    rows.append({"bucket": label, "payments": int(r.volume), "success rate": r.success_rate, "95% CI low": lo, "95% CI high": hi, "CI width (pts)": 100 * (hi - lo)})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4))
say("With only a few payments the interval is many points wide: a couple of failures prove nothing. "
    "This is why Lumio scales its z-scores by sampling noise and ignores segments with fewer than 30 payments for success-rate alerts.")
bucket payments success rate 95% CI low 95% CI high CI width (pts)
0 04:00 (quiet) 29 0.8621 0.6944 0.9450 25.0616
1 18:00 (busy) 252 0.9881 0.9656 0.9959 3.0353

With only a few payments the interval is many points wide: a couple of failures prove nothing. This is why Lumio scales its z-scores by sampling noise and ignores segments with fewer than 30 payments for success-rate alerts.

6. Linear regression¶

6.1 Simple linear regression: UPI payment time vs the UPI switch¶

y = β₀ + β₁·x + ε. Live period, 5-minute averages. Does the upstream service drive what customers feel?

In [26]:
u = (live[live.channel == "UPI"].groupby("ts").apply(lambda g: np.average(g.p95_ms, weights=g.volume)).rename("upi_payment_p95")
     .to_frame().join(svc[svc.service == "upi-switch"].set_index("ts").p95_ms.rename("upi_switch_p95")).dropna())
slr = smf.ols("upi_payment_p95 ~ upi_switch_p95", data=u).fit()
b0, b1 = slr.params; ci = slr.conf_int().loc["upi_switch_p95"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.2))
ax.scatter(u.upi_switch_p95, u.upi_payment_p95, s=6, alpha=.35, color=TEAL)
xs = np.linspace(u.upi_switch_p95.min(), u.upi_switch_p95.max(), 50); ax.plot(xs, b0 + b1 * xs, color=AMBER, lw=2)
ax.set(title=f"Simple linear regression  (R² = {slr.rsquared:.2f})", xlabel="UPI switch p95 (ms)", ylabel="UPI payment p95 (ms)"); plt.show()
RESULTS["slr"] = (b1, slr.rsquared)
say(f"**ŷ = {b0:.0f} + {b1:.2f}·x**  ·  R² = **{slr.rsquared:.3f}**  ·  r = {np.sqrt(slr.rsquared):.2f}  ·  slope 95 % CI [{ci[0]:.2f}, {ci[1]:.2f}], p = {slr.pvalues.iloc[1]:.3g}.  \n"
    f"Interpretation: every extra **1 ms** at the UPI switch adds about **{b1:.1f} ms** to the customer's payment time. "
    f"The switch explains {slr.rsquared:.0%} of the variation, so it is a key dependency to monitor.")

ŷ = 329 + 8.87·x · R² = 0.846 · r = 0.92 · slope 95 % CI [8.74, 9.01], p = 0.
Interpretation: every extra 1 ms at the UPI switch adds about 8.9 ms to the customer's payment time. The switch explains 85% of the variation, so it is a key dependency to monitor.

6.2 Confounding: does a bigger payment take longer?¶

avg_amount correlated ≈ 0.56 with p95 in the EDA. Add channel as a control and watch the effect disappear (omitted-variable bias).

In [27]:
smp = hist.sample(40_000, random_state=SEED)
m1 = smf.ols("p95_ms ~ avg_amount", data=smp).fit()
m2 = smf.ols("p95_ms ~ avg_amount + C(channel)", data=smp).fit()
display(pd.DataFrame({"model": ["p95 ~ amount", "p95 ~ amount + channel"],
                      "β(amount) ms per $": [m1.params["avg_amount"], m2.params["avg_amount"]],
                      "p-value": [m1.pvalues["avg_amount"], m2.pvalues["avg_amount"]],
                      "R²": [m1.rsquared, m2.rsquared]}).round(4))
say(f"Alone, each extra $1 seems to add **{m1.params['avg_amount']:.1f} ms**. Once channel is controlled, it is **{m2.params['avg_amount']:.2f} ms**. "
    "Card payments are both larger *and* slower; amount itself is not the cause. **Correlation is not causation**: always ask what else differs between the groups.")
model β(amount) ms per $ p-value R²
0 p95 ~ amount 18.1421 0.000 0.3109
1 p95 ~ amount + channel 0.4725 0.483 0.3230

Alone, each extra $1 seems to add 18.1 ms. Once channel is controlled, it is 0.47 ms. Card payments are both larger and slower; amount itself is not the cause. Correlation is not causation: always ask what else differs between the groups.

6.3 Multiple linear regression: what drives payment time?¶

log(p95) = β₀ + Σ β·(bank, channel, platform, region, hour, weekend, log volume, amount) + ε, fitted on the 3-week history. Using log(y) means each coefficient reads as an approximate % change: (e^β − 1) × 100.

In [28]:
formula = "log_p95 ~ C(bank) + C(channel) + C(platform) + C(region) + C(hour) + is_weekend + log_volume + avg_amount"
mlr = smf.ols(formula, data=hist).fit()
RESULTS["mlr_r2_train"] = mlr.rsquared
coef = pd.DataFrame({"coef": mlr.params, "p": mlr.pvalues, "ci_low": mlr.conf_int()[0], "ci_high": mlr.conf_int()[1]})
coef["effect_%"] = 100 * (np.exp(coef.coef) - 1); coef.loc["Intercept", "effect_%"] = np.nan
show = coef[~coef.index.str.startswith("C(hour)")]
display(show.round(4))
say(f"R² = **{mlr.rsquared:.3f}**, adjusted R² = {mlr.rsquared_adj:.3f}, F-test p = {mlr.f_pvalue:.3g}, n = {int(mlr.nobs):,}. "
    f"(23 hour coefficients hidden for space; they are plotted below.)")
hc = coef[coef.index.str.startswith("C(hour)")]["effect_%"]; hc.index = [int(i.split("T.")[1].rstrip("]")) for i in hc.index]
ax = pd.concat([pd.Series({0: 0.0}), hc]).sort_index().plot(kind="bar", color=TEAL, figsize=(11, 2.8), title="Hour-of-day effect on payment time vs midnight (%)")
ax.set(xlabel="hour", ylabel="%"); plt.show()

6.5 Out-of-sample evaluation + regression as an anomaly detector¶

Train = history; test = live period, normal rows only (rows touched by a planted event are excluded, so we measure how well the model knows normal).

7. Time-series analysis & forecasting¶

Series: total payments per hour, all segments, 17 Jan → 16 Feb 2025 (744 hours). Train = 3-week history (504 h), test = the 10 live days (240 h).

Walk-forward validation: every midnight of the test period we refit on everything known so far and forecast the next 24 hours, exactly how an operations team would use a forecast. This is more honest than one 240-hour forecast, and never lets the model see the future.

In [32]:

y_tr, y_te = y[:"2025-02-06 23:00"], y["2025-02-07":]
STORM = (pd.Timestamp("2025-02-10 14:00"), pd.Timestamp("2025-02-11 23:00"))

    if d.dayofweek >= 5: ax.axvspan(d, d + pd.Timedelta("1D"), color=GREY, alpha=.12, lw=0)
ax.axvspan(*STORM, color=BLUE, alpha=.12, lw=0, label="winter storm (real NAB)")

7.1 Decomposition (MSTL: trend + daily + weekly seasonality + remainder)¶

7.2 Stationarity: ADF and KPSS¶

In [34]:
def stationarity(s, name):
    s = s.dropna()
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        adf_p = adfuller(s, autolag="AIC")[1]
        kpss_p = kpss(s, regression="c", nlags="auto")[1]
    concl = ("stationary" if adf_p < .05 and kpss_p >= .05 else "non-stationary" if adf_p >= .05 and kpss_p < .05
             else "inconclusive (tests disagree)")
    return {"series": name, "ADF p  (H₀: unit root / non-stationary)": round(adf_p, 4),
            "KPSS p  (H₀: stationary)": "≥ 0.10" if kpss_p >= .1 else round(kpss_p, 4), "conclusion": concl}
ly = np.log(y)
st = pd.DataFrame([stationarity(ly[:"2025-02-06 23:00"], "log volume"),
                   stationarity(ly.diff(24)[:"2025-02-06 23:00"], "daily difference (lag 24)"),
                   stationarity(ly.diff(168)[:"2025-02-06 23:00"], "weekly difference (lag 168)")])
display(st)
say("ADF and KPSS have **opposite null hypotheses**, so agreement between them is strong evidence. "
    f"Log volume is judged **{st.conclusion[0]}**: there is no wandering trend (unit root). "
    "But stationarity in this sense does not mean 'no pattern': the mean still depends on the hour and the weekday, as the ACF below shows. "
    "We remove that by **seasonal differencing at lag 168** (this hour minus the same hour last week), which captures the daily *and* weekly rhythm in one step. "
    f"For the weekly-differenced series the tests say **{st.conclusion[2]}**: no unit root, but some short-term autocorrelation remains, which is exactly what the ARMA part of the model handles.")
series ADF p  (H₀: unit root / non-stationary) KPSS p  (H₀: stationary) conclusion
0 log volume 0.0 ≥ 0.10 stationary
1 daily difference (lag 24) 0.0 ≥ 0.10 stationary
2 weekly difference (lag 168) 0.0 0.01 inconclusive (tests disagree)

ADF and KPSS have opposite null hypotheses, so agreement between them is strong evidence. Log volume is judged stationary: there is no wandering trend (unit root). But stationarity in this sense does not mean 'no pattern': the mean still depends on the hour and the weekday, as the ACF below shows. We remove that by seasonal differencing at lag 168 (this hour minus the same hour last week), which captures the daily and weekly rhythm in one step. For the weekly-differenced series the tests say inconclusive (tests disagree): no unit root, but some short-term autocorrelation remains, which is exactly what the ARMA part of the model handles.

7.4 Model selection (AIC / BIC) and walk-forward forecasting¶

Model Idea
Seasonal naive "Same hour last week" (the benchmark any model must beat)
Holt-Winters (ETS) Exponential smoothing of log volume with an additive weekly seasonal pattern
SARIMA(p,0,q)(0,1,0)₁₆₈ + payday Weekly-differenced log volume, an ARMA model for what is left, and a payday-evening regressor (a known calendar event, so it is legitimate to tell the model about it in advance)

Choosing the ARMA order. We compute AIC/BIC (in-sample fit, penalised for complexity) and a validation MAPE: walk-forward day-ahead forecasts over the last training week (31 Jan – 6 Feb), still inside the history. Because our goal is forecasting, the order is chosen on validation error, so the live days remain an untouched test set.

In [36]:
pay_h = pd.Series((y.index.normalize().isin(pd.to_datetime(["2025-01-31", "2025-02-14"])) & (y.index.hour >= 15)).astype(float), index=y.index)
dpay = (pay_h - pay_h.shift(168)).fillna(0).rename("payday")   # the regressor, differenced the same way as y
z_tr = z[:"2025-02-06 23:00"].dropna()
def sarima_wf(order, days, alpha=.05):
    # walk-forward day-ahead SARIMA(order)(0,1,0)168 forecasts: refit every midnight on everything known so far
    pts, los, his = [], [], []
    for d in days:
        cut, idx = d - pd.Timedelta("1h"), pd.date_range(d, periods=24, freq="h"); zt = z[:cut].dropna()
        with warnings.catch_warnings():
            warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
            f = ARIMA(zt, exog=dpay[zt.index], order=order, trend="n").fit().get_forecast(24, exog=dpay[idx])
        base = ly.shift(168).loc[idx].values; ci = f.conf_int(alpha=alpha).values
        pts.append(pd.Series(np.exp(f.predicted_mean.values + base), idx))
        los.append(pd.Series(np.exp(ci[:, 0] + base), idx)); his.append(pd.Series(np.exp(ci[:, 1] + base), idx))
    return pd.concat(pts), pd.concat(los), pd.concat(his)
val_days = pd.date_range("2025-01-31", "2025-02-06")
cands = [(1, 0, 0), (2, 0, 0), (3, 0, 0), (1, 0, 1), (2, 0, 1), (1, 0, 2)]
rows, fits = [], {}
for o in cands:
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        fits[o] = ARIMA(z_tr, exog=dpay[z_tr.index], order=o, trend="n").fit()
    pv = sarima_wf(o, val_days)[0]; av = y.loc[pv.index]
    rows.append({"ARMA order (p,d,q)": str(o), "AIC": fits[o].aic, "BIC": fits[o].bic, "validation MAPE %": 100 * np.mean(np.abs(av - pv) / av)})
sel = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("ARMA order (p,d,q)").round(2)
best_order = cands[int(np.argmin(sel["validation MAPE %"].values))]
aic_order = cands[int(np.argmin(sel["AIC"].values))]
sel["lowest AIC"] = ["✔" if o == aic_order else "" for o in cands]
sel["chosen (validation)"] = ["✔" if o == best_order else "" for o in cands]
display(sel)
SAR = f"SARIMA{best_order}(0,1,0)₁₆₈"
say(f"Chosen: **{SAR} + payday regressor**." + (
    f" Note that AIC prefers {aic_order}: AIC rewards *in-sample* fit, while validation measures what we care about, accuracy on days the model has not seen. "
    "When they disagree, trust the out-of-sample measure for forecasting." if aic_order != best_order else " AIC and validation agree."))
print(fits[best_order].summary().tables[1])

8. Classification: logistic regression for incident detection¶

Unit: segment × 15-minute scan (the live app's scan interval). Label: 1 if the segment is inside a real incident window (from the answer key, used only for supervision and evaluation).

Features (all expected vs actual, so they are seasonal-aware):

Feature Definition
lat_z Regression residual of log p95 (Section 6) ÷ σ
fail_z (expected success − actual success) ÷ binomial standard error
vol_drop, vol_jump Negative / positive part of log(actual ÷ expected volume)

Split by time (never shuffle time-series data): train = Fri 7 – Tue 11, test = Wed 12 – Sun 16.

In [39]:
L = live.copy()
L["resid"] = L.log_p95 - mlr.predict(L)
L["bucket"] = L.ts.dt.floor("15min")
p0 = hist.groupby("segment", observed=True).apply(lambda g: g.success_count.sum() / g.volume.sum())
ev_vol = hist.groupby(["segment", "hour", "is_weekend"], observed=True).volume.mean()
L["exp_vol"] = ev_vol.reindex(pd.MultiIndex.from_frame(L[["segment", "hour", "is_weekend"]])).values
B = (L.groupby(["bucket"] + SEG + ["segment"], observed=True)
       .agg(volume=("volume", "sum"), success=("success_count", "sum"), exp_vol=("exp_vol", "sum"), resid=("resid", "mean"), p95_ms=("p95_ms", "mean"), n=("ts", "size"))
       .reset_index())
B = B[B.n == 3]                      # complete scans only (the data-quality gate)
B["p0"] = B.segment.map(p0).astype(float)
B["lat_z"] = B.resid / sigma
B["fail_z"] = (B.p0 - B.success / B.volume) / np.sqrt(B.p0 * (1 - B.p0) / B.volume)
lv = np.log(B.volume / B.exp_vol); B["vol_drop"], B["vol_jump"] = (-lv).clip(lower=0), lv.clip(lower=0)
B["ts"] = B.bucket
inc = key[key.kind == "incident"].reset_index(drop=True)
B["y"] = 0
for _, e in inc.iterrows():
    B.loc[in_scope(B, e.scope) & ((B.bucket + pd.Timedelta("15min") > e.start) & (B.bucket < e.end)).values, "y"] = 1
FEAT = ["lat_z", "fail_z", "vol_drop", "vol_jump"]
split = pd.Timestamp("2025-02-12")
tr, te = B[B.bucket < split], B[B.bucket >= split]

8.1 Comparing detectors: fixed threshold vs z-score vs logistic regression¶

  • Fixed threshold: p95 > 3,000 ms or success < 97 % (what most dashboards do)
  • z-score rule: lat_z > 3 or fail_z > 3 or |log volume ratio| > 1 (Lumio's statistical core, before its extra guardrails)
  • Logistic regression at a threshold chosen on the training data for F1

Two levels of evaluation: scan level (each segment × 15 min) and event level (was each incident caught, and how fast?).

In [42]:
pr_t, rc_t, th_t = precision_recall_curve(tr.y, logit.predict_proba(tr[FEAT])[:, 1])
f1_t = 2 * pr_t * rc_t / (pr_t + rc_t + 1e-9); best_th = th_t[np.argmax(f1_t[:-1])]
rules = {
    "Fixed threshold": ((te.p95_ms > 3000) | (te.success / te.volume < .97)).astype(int),
    "z-score rule":    ((te.lat_z > 3) | (te.fail_z > 3) | (te.vol_drop > 1) | (te.vol_jump > 1)).astype(int),
    f"Logistic (thr {best_th:.2f})": (te.prob >= best_th).astype(int)}
inc_te = inc[inc.start >= split]
def event_level(flag):
    out = []
    for _, e in inc_te.iterrows():
        m = in_scope(te, e.scope) & ((te.bucket + pd.Timedelta("15min") > e.start) & (te.bucket < e.end)).values & (flag.values == 1)
        first = te.bucket[m].min()
        out.append(np.nan if pd.isna(first) else max(0, (first + pd.Timedelta("15min") - e.start).total_seconds() / 60))
    return np.array(out)
days = te.bucket.dt.normalize().nunique()
rows = []
for name, fl in rules.items():
    ttd = event_level(fl)
    rows.append({"detector": name, "precision": precision_score(te.y, fl, zero_division=0), "recall": recall_score(te.y, fl), "F1": f1_score(te.y, fl),
                 "incidents caught": f"{np.isfinite(ttd).sum()}/{len(ttd)}", "median minutes to detect": np.nanmedian(ttd) if np.isfinite(ttd).any() else np.nan,
                 "false-alarm scans / day": ((fl == 1) & (te.y == 0)).sum() / days})
cmp = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("detector").round(3); display(cmp); RESULTS["detectors"] = cmp

There is no free lunch: every threshold trades missed incidents against false alarms. The right point is a business decision (cost of a missed incident vs the cost of waking someone up). Section 11 puts money on that trade-off.

Why does the production system add more than a classifier? A per-scan model still produces scattered false positives across 48 segments × 96 scans a day. Lumio adds (1) a data-quality gate, (2) grouping of segments into one story, (3) confirmation over 2 scans, (4) the change calendar for planned maintenance and (5) breadth checks for demand events. Over the full 10 days the live app scores 19/19 planted events with zero false alarms (see its Proof tab), against ~4,900 pages from a fixed rule. Section 11.4 simulates why confirmation is so powerful.

9. Machine learning & explainability¶

Lumio's production model is a gradient-boosted tree (HistGradientBoosting). Is it better than linear regression, and can we explain it?

Time-series cross-validation: each fold trains on the past and tests on the next block, never on the future. This avoids data leakage.

In [44]:
F_ML = ["bank", "channel", "platform", "region", "hour", "dow", "is_weekend", "log_volume", "avg_amount"]
def to_X(df):
    X = df[F_ML].copy()
    for c in SEG: X[c] = X[c].cat.codes
    for c in ["hour", "dow", "is_weekend"]: X[c] = X[c].astype(float)
    return X
H = hist.sort_values("ts"); Xh, yh = to_X(H), H.log_p95
Xlin = pd.get_dummies(H[F_ML].assign(hour=H.hour.astype(str), dow=H.dow.astype(str)), drop_first=True).astype(float)
cat_mask = [c in SEG for c in F_ML]
hgb = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=300, learning_rate=.08, categorical_features=cat_mask, random_state=SEED)
tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)
cv_rows = []
for name, model, X in [("Linear regression", LinearRegression(), Xlin), ("Gradient boosting", hgb, Xh)]:
    s = cross_validate(model, X, yh, cv=tscv, scoring=["r2", "neg_root_mean_squared_error"])
    cv_rows.append({"model": name, "CV R² mean": s["test_r2"].mean(), "CV R² sd": s["test_r2"].std(), "CV RMSE (log)": -s["test_neg_root_mean_squared_error"].mean()})
cvt = pd.DataFrame(cv_rows).set_index("model").round(4); display(cvt)

10. Clustering & segmentation (K-means + PCA)¶

Can we group the 48 segments by operational behaviour, without telling the algorithm their labels? Each segment is described by five features from the history:

Feature Meaning
p95 Average payment time
variability Coefficient of variation of p95 (how jumpy it is)
success Overall success rate
amount Average payment value
log_size Log of average volume per 5 minutes

(We first tried the 24-hour demand shape as features too, but every segment follows the same real NAB demand rhythm, so those features carried no information and only added noise. Feature selection is part of the analysis.)

11. Monte Carlo simulation¶

Monte Carlo answers questions that have uncertain inputs by simulating thousands of possible futures and looking at the distribution of outcomes, not just one average.

11.1 Step 1: measure what an incident costs, from the data¶

For each real incident in the live period:

  • Excess failed payments = actual failures − (expected failure rate × volume)
  • Vanished payments, measured with difference-in-differences: how far the affected segments' volume fell below expectation beyond how far the unaffected segments (the control group) fell in the same window. Without a control group, a quiet Sunday night or the storm would be wrongly counted as lost payments.
  • Value at risk = (excess failed + vanished) × average payment value, then divided by the incident's minutes.
In [48]:
rows = []
for _, e in inc.iterrows():
    m = in_scope(live, e.scope) & ((live.ts >= e.start) & (live.ts < e.end)).values
    d = live[m]
    exp_fail = (d.volume * (1 - d.segment.map(p0).astype(float))).sum()
    excess_fail = max(0, d.failed.sum() - exp_fail)
    # vanished payments: difference-in-differences against the unaffected segments (control group) in the same window
    ctrl = live[~m & ((live.ts >= e.start) & (live.ts < e.end)).values]
    expv = lambda x: ev_vol.reindex(pd.MultiIndex.from_frame(x[["segment", "hour", "is_weekend"]])).values.sum()
    exp_in = expv(d); ratio_in, ratio_ctrl = d.volume.sum() / exp_in, ctrl.volume.sum() / expv(ctrl)
    lost = max(0, (ratio_ctrl - ratio_in) * exp_in) if ratio_ctrl - ratio_in > .05 else 0   # ignore < 5 pts (noise)
    minutes = (e.end - e.start).total_seconds() / 60
    value = (excess_fail + lost) * d.avg_amount.mean()
    rows.append({"incident": e["name"][:48], "minutes": minutes, "excess failed": round(excess_fail), "vanished payments": round(lost),
                 "value at risk $": round(value), "$ per minute": round(value / minutes, 1)})
impact = pd.DataFrame(rows); display(impact)
RATE = impact["$ per minute"].values
say(f"Median **${np.median(RATE):,.0f} per minute** of incident, max **${RATE.max():,.0f}**. Latency-only incidents show $0 here because slow-but-successful payments are not counted as lost. "
    "That is a deliberately **conservative** choice (in reality some customers abandon a slow payment).")

11.2 Step 2: the simulation model¶

Loss per incident = loss rate ($/min) × (time to detect + time to fix)

Input Distribution Source
Incidents per year Poisson(λ = 48, i.e. 4 per month) Assumption (the demo is deliberately denser)
Loss rate $/min Bootstrap from the measured incidents above × LogNormal(0, 0.3) noise Data (Section 11.1)
Time to detect, without Lumio LogNormal, median 90 min, σ = 0.5 Assumption: customer complaints / manual dashboard checks
Time to detect, with Lumio LogNormal, median 30 min, σ = 0.3 Data: 2 confirmed 15-min scans (live app)
Lumio misses an incident Bernoulli(5 %) → falls back to "without" Assumption (conservative: 0 misses in the demo)
Time to fix after detection LogNormal, median 45 min, σ = 0.6 (same in both worlds) Assumption (conservative: ignores Lumio's root-cause help)
Annual cost of running Lumio $150,000 Assumption

10,000 simulated years.

In [49]:
BASE = dict(lam=48, ttd0=90, ttd1=30, fix=45, miss=.05, rate_mult=1.0, cost=150_000)
def simulate(n=10_000, seed=SEED, **kw):
    p = {**BASE, **kw}; g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    k = g.poisson(p["lam"], n); sim = np.repeat(np.arange(n), k); N = k.sum()
    rate = g.choice(RATE, N) * g.lognormal(0, .3, N) * p["rate_mult"]
    fix = g.lognormal(np.log(p["fix"]), .6, N)
    t0 = g.lognormal(np.log(p["ttd0"]), .5, N)
    t1 = np.where(g.random(N) < p["miss"], t0, g.lognormal(np.log(p["ttd1"]), .3, N))
    without = np.bincount(sim, rate * (t0 + fix), minlength=n); with_ = np.bincount(sim, rate * (t1 + fix), minlength=n)
    return pd.DataFrame({"loss_without": without, "loss_with": with_, "saving": without - with_, "net_benefit": without - with_ - p["cost"]})
t0 = time.time(); mc = simulate(); print(f"10,000 years simulated in {time.time()-t0:.2f}s")
pct = mc.quantile([.05, .5, .95]).T; pct["mean"] = mc.mean(); pct.columns = ["P5", "P50 (median)", "P95", "mean"]
display((pct / 1e6).round(2).rename(lambda s: s + " ($M)"))
p_pos = (mc.net_benefit > 0).mean(); RESULTS["mc"] = (mc.saving.median(), p_pos, mc.net_benefit.quantile(.05))

11.4 Monte Carlo for alert design: why one scan is never enough¶

Normal noise only, no incidents at all. 48 segments × 3 signals × 96 scans a day = 13,824 checks a day. Noise is autocorrelated (AR(1), ρ = 0.5). How many false pages per day does each rule produce?

In [53]:
g = np.random.default_rng(SEED); DAYS, SCANS, CH, rho = 200, 96, 48 * 3, .5
eps = g.standard_normal((DAYS * SCANS, CH)); z = np.empty_like(eps); z[0] = eps[0]
for t in range(1, len(z)): z[t] = rho * z[t - 1] + np.sqrt(1 - rho**2) * eps[t]
def pages_per_day(trig): return trig.reshape(DAYS, SCANS, CH).sum(axis=(1, 2))
rules = {"z > 2, single scan": z > 2, "z > 3, single scan": z > 3,
         "z > 3, 2 scans in a row": (z[1:] > 3) & (z[:-1] > 3), "z > 2.5, 2 scans in a row": (z[1:] > 2.5) & (z[:-1] > 2.5)}
fa = []
for name, trig in rules.items():
    if trig.shape[0] < DAYS * SCANS: trig = np.vstack([np.zeros((1, CH), bool), trig])
    ppd = pages_per_day(trig)
    fa.append({"rule": name, "false pages / day (mean)": ppd.mean(), "days with zero false pages": (ppd == 0).mean(),
               "simulated P(one check fires)": trig.mean(), "theory P(one check fires)": np.nan})
fa = pd.DataFrame(fa).set_index("rule")
fa.loc["z > 2, single scan", "theory P(one check fires)"] = 1 - stats.norm.cdf(2)
fa.loc["z > 3, single scan", "theory P(one check fires)"] = 1 - stats.norm.cdf(3)
display(fa.round(4)); RESULTS["mc_alert"] = fa
say(f"Even a strict z > 3 fires **{fa.iloc[1,0]:.0f} false pages a day** across 13,824 checks: the **multiple-comparisons problem**. "
    f"Requiring confirmation on 2 consecutive scans cuts that to **{fa.iloc[2,0]:.1f}**. Adding grouping, minimum volume and the data-quality gate is how the live app reaches zero. "
    "The simulation also checks the theory: the simulated single-scan rates match the normal-distribution tail probabilities.")
false pages / day (mean) days with zero false pages simulated P(one check fires) theory P(one check fires)
rule
z > 2, single scan 316.545 0.00 0.0229 0.0228
z > 3, single scan 19.120 0.00 0.0014 0.0013
z > 3, 2 scans in a row 1.155 0.36 0.0001 NaN

Even a strict z > 3 fires 19 false pages a day across 13,824 checks: the multiple-comparisons problem. Requiring confirmation on 2 consecutive scans cuts that to 1.2. Adding grouping, minimum volume and the data-quality gate is how the live app reaches zero. The simulation also checks the theory: the simulated single-scan rates match the normal-distribution tail probabilities.

12. Ethics, privacy & governance¶

Principle How this project applies it
Data minimisation & privacy Only aggregated telemetry (counts, rates, timings per segment per 5 min). No customer names, card numbers or account data ever enter the analysis. In production, segment data would be pseudonymised and access-controlled (PIPEDA in Canada, GDPR, PCI-DSS for card data).
Fairness Thresholds are learned per segment, so a smaller bank or quieter region is not ignored, or over-alerted, just because it is small (Sections 5.5, 8).
Transparency / explainability Every alert states the evidence (charts, the test used, the p-value). Gradient-boosting results are explained with importance and partial dependence (Section 9).
Human in the loop Lumio recommends; people decide. Actions such as pause rollout or block pattern need a click from the accountable team, and every action is logged.
AI accountability When the AI agent proposes a cause, the claim must pass a statistical test (Fisher / Mann-Whitney) before it is shown. No test, no claim: it says "cause unknown" instead of guessing.
Honest evaluation The answer key is never used to tune detection rules; train/test splits are by time; assumptions in the business case are labelled and stress-tested.
Data provenance & licensing NAB data used under its MIT licence and cited; simulated components are clearly declared.

Key results¶

Question Answer from the data
Q1 · What is normal? Strong daily + weekly seasonality (strength 0.99 / 0.98); busiest hour ≈ 19× the quietest
Q2 · Do groups differ? Bank matters (η² = 17.4%, large); Android vs iOS is a small effect (d = 0.34); channel vs failure is significant but negligible (Cramér's V = 0.0072)
Q3 · What drives payment time? UPI switch alone explains R² = 0.85 of UPI payment time; multiple regression R² = 0.64 (train) / 0.61 (unseen live data); gradient boosting R² = 0.62
Q3b · Root cause App v5.2 is 3.2× slower than v5.1 (Mann-Whitney, p < 0.001)
Q4 · Forecasting Best model SARIMA(1, 0, 1)(0,1,0)₁₆₈, MAPE 5.9 % on normal days (15 % lower error than seasonal naive); 82% of storm hours fall outside the 95 % interval vs 6% of other hours
Q5 · Detection Fixed threshold: precision 0.11, 643 false-alarm scans/day · z-score rule: precision 0.63, recall 0.97, 47/day · logistic ROC-AUC 0.998. All caught 5/5 test incidents; the full live app (with grouping + confirmation) scores 19/19 with zero false alarms
Q6 · Segments K-means finds 4 behavioural clusters
Q7 · Is it worth it? Median saving $5.50M / year for this network; P(net benefit > 0) = 100.0%; still positive in most years down to ~5% of this size

Limitations (be the first to say them)¶

  1. Simulated payments. The rhythm and three anomalies are real (NAB), but payment outcomes are simulated. Results show the method works; a pilot on a real bank's data is the next step.
  2. One season. Three weeks of history cannot learn yearly patterns (holidays, tax season). Production needs 12+ months.
  3. Planted incidents are known types. A truly novel failure may look different; that is why the app includes the AI agent and "cause unknown".
  4. Autocorrelation. Rows close in time are not independent, so classical p-values are optimistic. We mitigated this with hourly units, time-based splits and time-series CV.
  5. Business-case assumptions. Incident frequency, detection time without Lumio and tool cost are assumptions, which is why we show their sensitivity.

Recommendations¶

  1. Use expected-vs-actual (regression / ML baselines) instead of fixed thresholds for every payment KPI.
  2. Require statistical evidence + 2-scan confirmation before paging people.
  3. Treat system-wide demand swings (storms, paydays) as advisories, not incidents.
  4. Run a 90-day pilot with one bank to validate the Monte Carlo assumptions, then re-run Section 11 with real numbers.
  5. Re-train baselines monthly and monitor for model drift (performance falling on recent data).

14. Professor's likely questions — and how to answer them¶

A. Problem & project design¶

1. Why is this a data analytics problem and not just an IT monitoring problem? Because the failures are statistical: every server is "up", but a slice of customers sees slower or failed payments. Spotting them needs baselines, seasonality, hypothesis tests and segmentation, which is analytics work, not uptime checks.

2. Which methodology did you follow? CRISP-DM (Section 0): business understanding → data understanding → preparation → modelling → evaluation → deployment (the live app).

3. Who are the stakeholders and how does your output reach them? Ops/SRE, Release, Fraud, Business Operations, Leadership (Section 0.2). The live app routes each alert by e-mail to the responsible department, with evidence and action buttons.

4. How did you define success before you started? Section 0.4: R² ≥ 0.5 on unseen data, MAPE ≤ 10 %, catching every test incident with fewer false alarms than a fixed rule, and a positive expected net benefit. Section 13 reports against these.

B. Data¶

5. Is the data real? Partly, and that is deliberate. Volume rhythm, a blizzard, a system failure and a database level-shift come from the Numenta Anomaly Benchmark (real, labelled). Payment outcomes are simulated on top so the ground truth is known exactly. Real bank data is confidential and unlabelled, so you could not measure precision and recall honestly with it.

6. How did you handle missing data and duplicates? Duplicates removed; gaps not filled with zeros, because a zero would fake an outage. IQR outliers kept because they are real peak behaviour (Section 2).

7. Why use p95 instead of the average payment time? Latency is right-skewed; the 95th percentile captures the slow tail customers actually feel and is the industry-standard SLI.

8. Why did you log-transform payment time? To reduce skew, stabilise variance and make coefficients read as % effects (Section 6.3).

C. Statistics¶

9. Your p-values are all tiny. Does that mean everything matters? No. With ~40 M payments, tiny differences are significant. That is why we report effect sizes (Cohen's d, η², Cramér's V). Channel vs failure is significant but negligible (Section 5.2).

10. Why Welch's t-test instead of Student's t-test? Levene's test showed unequal variances; Welch does not assume them.

11. Why Mann-Whitney for the release comparison? p95 values are skewed and the samples are small, so a non-parametric test is safer. Fisher's exact test is used for failure counts in a 2×2 table.

12. Isn't running many tests a multiple-comparisons problem? Yes. Section 11.4 simulates it: 13,824 checks a day at z > 3 still give dozens of false pages a day. We control it with confirmation over 2 scans, grouping and minimum-volume rules, the operational equivalent of a family-wise correction. In a purely academic setting, Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg would be the textbook fixes.

D. Regression¶

13. Interpret one coefficient for me. Use Section 6.3, e.g. "Holding bank, region, hour and load constant, UPI payments are about X % faster than card payments", where X comes from the coefficient table.

14. Did you check the regression assumptions? Yes (Section 6.4): residual plot, Q-Q plot, Breusch-Pagan (heteroscedasticity → robust HC3 errors), Durbin-Watson (autocorrelation in time data), VIF (multicollinearity).

15. What is confounding, and where did you see it? Amount appeared to slow payments, but card payments are both bigger and slower. Adding channel removed the effect (Section 6.2). This is omitted-variable bias.

16. Why is R² on training data different from R² on the test data? Test data is unseen and from a different period. A small drop is normal; a large drop would mean overfitting. We report both (6.3, 6.5).

17. Linear regression vs gradient boosting: which would you deploy, and why? Gradient boosting fits better (captures interactions), and we explain it with permutation importance and partial dependence. Linear regression stays as the interpretable benchmark and the teaching model (Section 9).

E. Time series¶

18. What is stationarity and why does it matter? Constant mean and variance over time; ARIMA-type models assume it. ADF and KPSS (opposite nulls) show seasonal differencing is needed (Section 7.2).

19. How did you choose the SARIMA orders? The ACF shows 24 h and 168 h seasonality, so we difference by one week (D = 1, s = 168). The PACF of the differenced series suggests a low order, and we compared candidate ARMA orders by AIC and by validation MAPE on the last training week, choosing by validation because the goal is forecasting (Section 7.4). A payday regressor was added. It was then tested walk-forward on the 10 live days against seasonal naive and Holt-Winters.

19b. AIC picked a different model from validation. Which is right? AIC measures in-sample fit with a complexity penalty; validation measures accuracy on unseen days. For a forecasting goal, out-of-sample performance wins, and here the validation choice also did better on the test days.

20. What is walk-forward validation and why use it? Each day we refit on everything known up to midnight and forecast the next 24 hours, which is how the forecast would be used in operations. It never lets the model see the future, and it tests the model 10 separate times instead of once.

20b. Why exclude the storm when measuring forecast accuracy? No model should predict a blizzard from payment history. We measure accuracy on normal hours, then show the storm is detected because it falls outside the prediction interval (Section 7.5).

21. Why not shuffle the data for cross-validation? Shuffling leaks the future into training. We use time-based splits and TimeSeriesSplit.

F. Classification & evaluation¶

22. Why not report accuracy? Only about 2–4 % of scans are inside an incident: a model that always says "normal" would be over 96 % accurate and completely useless. We use precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and PR-AUC.

23. Precision or recall: which matters more here? Both have a cost: a missed incident loses money; a false alarm wastes people's time and erodes trust (alert fatigue). The threshold curve (Section 8.1) shows the trade-off, and the Monte Carlo puts dollars on it.

24. How do you interpret the logistic-regression odds ratios? The multiplier on the odds of a real incident per 1-SD rise in a feature (Section 8).

25. Your logistic model was trained with labels. Doesn't that use the answer key? Only for this classroom comparison, and only on the training days. The live app's detector never sees labels; it uses the unsupervised expected-vs-actual rules and is scored afterwards.

G. Clustering & Monte Carlo¶

26. How did you pick k in K-means? Elbow method plus silhouette score (Section 10). The silhouette peaks at k = 2, but that is just UPI vs Card, which we already knew. k = 4 still has reasonable separation and reveals a high-traffic/fast vs low-traffic/slow tier inside each channel, which is actionable. Features were standardised first because K-means uses distances. We also dropped the demand-shape features after finding they carried no information.

27. Why Monte Carlo and not just one ROI number? The inputs are uncertain. Monte Carlo gives a distribution: median saving, probability of a positive return, a bad-year (5th percentile) case, and the bank size where the case breaks even (Section 11).

27b. How did you measure the cost of an incident? From the data: excess failures against the segment's normal failure rate, plus vanished payments measured by difference-in-differences against unaffected segments (a control group). Without the control group, a quiet Sunday night or the storm would be miscounted as lost money.

28. How many simulations are enough? Until the running mean stabilises. The convergence plot shows the CI narrowing as 1/√n; 10,000 is well past that.

29. Which assumption matters most? The tornado chart (Section 11.3) ranks them, which tells the bank what to measure first in a pilot.

H. Ethics, limitations & future work¶

30. Any privacy concerns? Only aggregated, non-personal telemetry is used; production would add pseudonymisation and access controls (PIPEDA / GDPR / PCI-DSS). See Section 12.

31. What are the main limitations? Simulated outcomes, one season of history, known incident types, autocorrelation and business-case assumptions (Section 13).

32. If you had 3 more months, what would you do? Pilot on one bank's real data; 12 months of history for yearly seasonality; drift monitoring and monthly retraining; validate the Monte Carlo inputs; A/B-test alert thresholds with the on-call team.

33. What did you personally learn? (Answer in your own words.) For example: that "significant" isn't "important", that the baseline matters more than the threshold, and that the hardest part of analytics is turning a number into an action someone takes.

Data: Numenta Anomaly Benchmark (Lavin & Ahmad, 2015; MIT licence) + simulated payments. Methods: pandas, SQLite, SciPy, statsmodels, scikit-learn.
